swaddle.e: From Middle English swathlen (“to bind; swaddle”), from Middle English swathel, swethel, from Old English swaþul, swæþel, sweþel, sweoþol (“swaddling cloth”), equivalent to swathe (“to wrap with fabric”) + -le (agent/instrumental suffix), the word then underwent th-stopping (its voiced th became a d).
swaddle.g: To bind (a baby) with long narrow strips of cloth.

swaddling.e: From Middle English swaþelynge; equivalent to swaddle + -ing.
swaddling.g: The practice of wrapping infants in clothing that restricts movement.

swallow.e: From Middle English swolwen, from Old English swelgan, from Proto-West Germanic *swelgan, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą (“to swallow, revel, devour”), from Proto-Indo-European *swelk- (“to gulp”).
swallow.g: To cause (food, drink etc.) to pass from the mouth into the stomach; to take into the stomach through the throat.

swallow.e: From Middle English swalwe, swalewe, swalowe, from Old English swealwe, from Proto-West Germanic *swalwā, from Proto-Germanic *swalwǭ.
swallow.g: A small migratory bird of the family Hirundinidae with long, pointed wings and a forked tail which feeds on the wing by catching insects.

swamp.e: Early attestations (starting in 1624) are from North America, but the term was probably in local use in Britain earlier. The etymology is not entirely certain; it is probably a fusion of Middle English swam (“swamp, muddy pool, bog, marsh”, also “fungus, mushroom”) — from Old English swamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), from Proto-West Germanic *swamm.
swamp.g: An area of wet (water-saturated), spongy (soft) land, often with trees, generally a rich ecosystem for certain plants and animals but ill-su

swan.e: From Middle English swan, from Old English swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”, literally “the singing bird”), from Proto-Indo-European *swonh₂-/*swenh₂- (“to sing, make sound”). Related also to Old English ġeswin (“melody, song”), Old English swinsian (“to make melody”).
swan.g: Any of various species of large, long-necked waterfowl, of genus Cygnus (bird family: Anatidae), most of which have white plumage.

swan.e: Probably from dialectal I s’wan, a corruption of I shall warrant; or possibly from a minced form of I swear on.
swan.g: To declare (chiefly in first-person present constructions).

swarm.e: From Middle English swarm, from Old English swearm (“swarm, multitude”), from Proto-West Germanic *swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz (“swarm, dizziness”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”).
swarm.g: A large number of insects or other bugs (e.g. centipedes), especially when in motion or (for bees) migrating to a new colony.

sway.e: From earlier swey (“to fall, swoon”), from Middle English sweyen, from Old English *swǣġan (“to bend, bow”), from Proto-West Germanic *swaigijan, from Proto-Germanic *swaigijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₁- See also Saterland Frisian swooie (“to swing, wave, wobble”).
sway.g: The act of swaying; a swaying motion; a swing or sweep of a weapon.

swear.e: From Middle English sweren, swerien, from Old English swerian (“to swear, take an oath of office”), from Proto-West Germanic *swarjan, from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to swear”). The original sense in all Germanic languages is “to take an oath”.
swear.g: To take an oath, to promise intensely, solemnly, and/or with legally binding effect.

swear.e: From the above verb, or from Middle English sware, from Old English swaru, from Proto-Germanic *swarō.

swearer.e: From Middle English swerere; equivalent to swear + -er.

swearing.e: From Middle English swerynge; equivalent to swear + -ing.
swearing.g: The act of swearing, or making an oath.

sweat.e: From Middle English swete, swet, swate, swote, from Old English swāt, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, *swaitą, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), o-grade of *sweyd- (“to sweat”).
sweat.g: Fluid that exits the body through pores in the skin usually due to physical stress and/or high temperature for the purpose of regulating bod

sweat.e: From Middle English sweten, from Old English swǣtan, from Proto-Germanic *swaitijaną (“to sweat”).

sweep.e: From Middle English swepen, from Proto-West Germanic *swaipijan (unattested in Old English), from Proto-Germanic *swaipijaną. More distantly related to Old Norse sveipa (whence Swedish svepa).
sweep.g: To clean (a surface) by means of a stroking motion of a broom or brush.

sweeps.g: The Nielsen ratings used to measure television show viewership several times a year.

sweet.e: From Middle English soot, sweete, swete, swoote, from Old English swēte, swoete, swōt, swœ̄te (“sweet”), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz (“sweet”), from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus (“sweet”), from *sweh₂d- (“sweet”) + *-us.

sweeten.e: From sweet + -en. Eclipsed non-native Middle English doucen and endoucen, borrowed from Old French adoucir and endoucir (“to sweeten”).
sweeten.g: To make sweet to the taste.

sweetly.e: From Middle English swetly, swetely, sweteliche, from Old English swētlīċe (“sweetly; pleasantly”), equivalent to sweet + -ly.
sweetly.g: With a sweet taste or aroma.

sweetness.e: From Middle English swetnes, swetnesse, from Old English swētnes (“sweetness”), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtinassī (“sweetness”), equivalent to sweet + -ness.
sweetness.g: The condition of being sweet (all senses).

swell.e: From Middle English swellen, from Old English swellan (“to swell”), from Proto-West Germanic *swellan, from Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”), of unknown origin. The adjective may derive from the noun.
swell.g: To become larger, fuller, or rounder, or expand in size or shape, usually as a result of pressure from within.

swell.e: From Middle English swelle, from the verb swellen (modern swell).
swell.g: The act of swelling; increase in size.

swerve.e: From Middle English swerven, swarven, from Old English sweorfan (“to file; rub; polish; scour; turn aside”), from Proto-Germanic *swerbaną (“to rub off; wipe; mop”), from Proto-Indo-European *swerbʰ- (“to turn; wipe; sweep”).
swerve.g: To stray; to wander; to rove.

swift.e: From Middle English swift, from Old English swift (“swift; quick”), from Proto-Germanic *swiftaz (“swift; quick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)weyp- (“to twist; wind around”).

swiftly.e: From Middle English swiftly, swyftely, swiftliche, from Old English swiftlīċe (“swiftly”), equivalent to swift + -ly.
swiftly.g: In a swift manner; quickly; with quick motion or velocity; fleetly.

swim.e: From Middle English swymmen, from Old English swimman (“to swim, float”) (class III strong verb; past tense swamm, past participle geswummen), from Proto-West Germanic *swimman, from Proto-Germanic *swimmaną (“to swim”), from Proto-Indo-European *swem(bʰ)- (“to be unsteady, move, swim”).
swim.g: To move through the water, without touching the bottom; to propel oneself in water by natural means.

swim.e: From Middle English swime, sweme, swaime (“a dizziness, swoon, trance”), from Old English swīma (“a swoon, swimming in the head”).

swimmer.e: From Middle English swimmere, equivalent to swim + -er. The dumplings are so called because they are often served in stew.

swimming.e: From Middle English swymmynge. Equivalent to swim (“to move through water”, verb) + -ing (suffix forming gerunds).
swimming.g: The act or art of sustaining and propelling the body in water.

swimming.e: From swim (“to be dizzy”, verb) + -ing (suffix forming gerunds).
swimming.g: The state of being dizzy or in vertigo.

swindler.g: A person who swindles, cheats or defrauds.

swine.e: From Middle English swyn, swin; from Old English swīn; from Proto-West Germanic *swīn; from Proto-Germanic *swīną; from an adjectival form of Proto-Indo-European *suH- (“pig”). In modern use, especially as a term of abuse, frequently a calque of German Schwein or its derivatives. In reference to wolffish, a clipping of swinefish.
swine.g: A pig, an animal of family Suidae, especially in agricultural contexts.

swing.e: From Middle English swyngen, from Old English swingan, from Proto-West Germanic *swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą (compare Low German swingen, German schwingen, Dutch zwingen, Swedish svinga), from Proto-Indo-European *swenk-, *sweng- (compare Scottish Gaelic seang (“thin”)).
swing.g: To rotate about an off-centre fixed point.

swinging.e: The sexual practice is so called after the custom in swing dancing of changing partners after each dance, unlike traditional ballroom dance styles where one has a single partner.
swinging.g: The act or motion of that which swings.

swirl.e: From Middle English swirlen (“to eddy, swirl”), probably from Old Norse *svirla (“to swirl”), a frequentative form of Old Norse sverra (“to swing, twirl”).
swirl.g: To twist or whirl, as an eddy.

swollen.e: From Middle English swollen, i-swolle, y-swolle, yswolle, ȝeswollen, from Old English swollen, ġeswollen, from Proto-Germanic *swullanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”).
swollen.g: Protuberant or abnormally distended (as by injury or disease).

swoon.e: From Middle English swoune, swone, from the verb (see below).

From Middle English swounen, swonen (“to faint”), and aswoune (“in a swoon”), both ultimately from Old English ġeswōgen (“insensible, senseless, dead”), past participle of swōgan (“to make a sound, overrun, suffocate”) (compare Old English āswōgan (“to cover over, overcome”)), from Proto-West Germanic *swōgan.

swoop.e: From Middle English swopen (“to sweep”), from Old English swāpan.
swoop.g: To fly or glide downwards suddenly; to plunge (in the air) or nosedive.

sword.e: From West Midland Middle English sword (swerd in most dialects), from Old English sweord (“sword”), from Proto-West Germanic *swerd (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *swerdą (“sword”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂w- (“sharp”).
sword.g: A long bladed weapon with a grip and typically a pommel and crossguard (together forming a hilt), which is designed to cut, stab, slash and/

sworn.e: From Middle English sworen, isworen, from Old English sworen, ġesworen, from Proto-West Germanic *swaran, *giswaran, from Proto-Germanic *swaranaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to swear”), equivalent to swear + -en.
